subject: SIG: Dedicated GPU dataflow and side-channel mitigations
messages:
From: Acme Security Team <security@acme-payments.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>
Date: Fri, 3 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SIG follow-up: dedicated GPU tenancy and dataflow questions

Ben —

Thanks for sending the initial SIG spreadsheet. A couple of follow-ups from the Acme security review team before we can sign off on dedicated GPU procurement:

1) Dataflow boundaries: in your SIG answers you noted that model weights and runtime cache live on the GPU. Can you outline the end-to-end dataflow when a request from Acme hits a dedicated pool? Specifically: network ingress path, host vs. device memory residency during generation, and any offload to host swap.

2) Side-channel mitigations: Acme needs assurance that tenants cannot observe timing or microarchitectural side channels (e.g., L2/L3 eviction patterns, power/thermal inference) that could be used to reconstruct workload fingerprints. Please summarize any mitigations or accepted residual risks.

3) KV-cache eviction and reuse: When a tenant's request is evicted from the in-GPU KV cache, is there any risk of ghosting (residual data accessible to other tenants) before memory is zeroed or reallocated? How long is memory zeroed and who controls the zeroing?

4) Evidence: a short diagram and any attestation or test artifacts would be helpful (even a controlled test plan). Are you able to provide a brief network/dataflow diagram and a note on the cryptographic separation controls?

We appreciate prompt clarification — procurement has a tight timeline.

Thanks,
Liam O'Neil
Security Engineer, Acme Payments
[Acme SSO: liam.oneil]

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>
To: Acme Security Team <security@acme-payments.com>
Cc: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood-inference.com>, Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood-inference.com>

Subject: Re: SIG follow-up: dedicated GPU tenancy and dataflow questions

Liam —

Thanks for the clear list. Quick summary up front: dedicated pools give you strong isolation guarantees at the orchestration, hypervisor, host, and GPU driver layers. We attach a short diagram and an internal attestation (kvcache-attestation.txt) as requested. Details below and next steps at the end.

1) Dataflow (high level)
- Ingress: requests land on a customer-dedicated fronting pod in the region you select. Networking uses tenant-specific VPC peering or private connectivity (no public NAT for the pod).
- Model weights: stored on disk in an encrypted model store and loaded into GPU device memory by the Redwood runtime at model load time. Loaded weights are pinned to device memory for the model instance.
- KV cache: per-request KV entries are allocated in device memory (reserved allocation per runtime instance). We do not spill user KV cache to host page files under normal operation; spill to host occurs only under explicit offload policies configured by the customer and only to encrypted host buffers.
- Output: generated tokens are streamed back over the fronting pod to your network peer; transient buffers exist on host only for network serialization.

2) Side-channel mitigations
- Scheduling: we use cgroup/cpuset isolation and deterministic slot scheduling for dedicated GPUs to reduce co-scheduling with noisy co-tenants.
- Driver hygiene: we rely on vendor driver features to prevent cross-context L2/L3 leakage where supported; where chipsets expose potential microarchitectural leakage, we deploy conservative scheduling and no simultaneous multi-tenant context sharing.
- Noise injection: for high-sensitivity workloads we can enable configurable request shaping that adds minimal timing noise to reduce fingerprinting surface — we can provide measurements on added latency.
- Monitoring: runtime telemetry includes microburst detection and anomaly alerts; if abnormal patterns consistent with side-channel probing are detected, the request stream is flagged and subject to mitigation (throttle/evict).

3) KV-cache eviction and memory zeroing
- KV cache is allocated from per-instance device pools. On eviction, the runtime overwrites the GPU allocation with a zero pattern before returning that allocation to the pool. The zeroing is synchronous with the free operation and visible in the runtime logs for attestations.
- We provide a reproducible test script that exercises eviction and scans freed allocations to demonstrate non-recoverability. See attached kvcache-attestation.txt for the test harness and results.

4) Evidence attached
- redwood_isolation_diagram.pdf (dataflow + where keys and caches live)
- kvcache-attestation.txt (test harness and sample logs)
- We will produce a short customer-facing SIG response PDF after internal review.

Next steps
- Internal: Priyom and Mina, please review the attached attestation and add any low-level hardware caveats.
- External: Liam, if this level of detail looks appropriate we can follow with a controlled test run in a sandbox dedicated pool and a short recorded run demonstrating eviction zeroing.

Ben
Ben Carter
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Ben / Mina —

A couple of suggestions before we send the final customer PDF:

- Can we be explicit about when host-offload can occur (specific config knobs) and that offload only uses encrypted host pinned buffers? Acme will ask whether offload could write to pagecache. Call out that offload is opt-in and requires tenant config.

- For the side-channel block, please add a short statement about supported GPU generations (e.g., Ampere/Blackwell) and a caveat for older hardware where microarch mitigations are incomplete. That avoids a later surprise.

- For the zeroing attestation, include the exact log snippet timestamps and the runtime invocation used to trigger the zeroing so the customer can reproduce in a sandbox.

I can take the attestation doc and add the log snippet; Mina can add the hardware caveats.

—Priyom

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>

Date: Mon, 6 Jul 2026 14:25:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: SIG follow-up: dedicated GPU dataflow and side-channel mitigations (final)

Liam —

Thanks for the patience. Per Priyom and Mina's notes we've updated the customer-facing packet and attached a concise Sig response PDF that includes the requested artifacts and reproducible steps. Key clarifications included:

- Host offload: explicitly opt-in via the "offload.policy" runtime flag. Offload writes only to encrypted, pinned host buffers (no writes to system swap or unencrypted pagecache). We call this out and include the config snippet in the PDF.
- Hardware caveats: our mitigation posture is documented by GPU family. For Blackwell-class hardware we leverage vendor-provided context isolation and microcode fixes; for older Ampere variants we add conservative scheduling and optional noise-injection. PDF table lists firmware/driver versions we certify.
- Zeroing attestation: included exact runtime command and the log snippet demonstrating synchronous zeroing of freed device allocations (timestamps in UTC).

Attachments: sig-response-acme-20260706.pdf, redwood_isolation_diagram.pdf, kvcache-attestation.txt

If you'd like, we can run a short sandbox test (30–60 minutes) in a dedicated pool and provide you the raw logs — we recommend scheduling it this week.

Best,
Ben Carter
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
